topics.title: Exception Safety Guarantees (Basic, Strong, Nothrow)
topics.description: Mastering the 3 levels of exception safety: Basic guarantee, Strong (Commit-or-Rollback), and Nothrow.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content:
Exception Safety Guarantees define the state of an application if an exception is thrown during an operation:
• Basic Guarantee: No resources leaked; objects remain in valid states.
• Strong Guarantee: Commit-or-Rollback (if operation fails, state is rolled back to exactly what it was before).
• Nothrow Guarantee (noexcept): Operation is guaranteed never to fail or throw.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Without exception safety, partial failures leave objects corrupted, invariants broken, and resources leaked.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Use Copy-and-Swap idiom to achieve the Strong Exception Guarantee.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Perform all risky allocations in temporary objects. Once successful, swap state using noexcept swap.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Aim for Strong Exception Guarantee on all critical state mutations.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Predictable, resilient software that recovers from errors gracefully.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Copy-and-swap can require temporary allocations.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Basic, Strong, Nothrow, Destructor noexcept.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Throwing exceptions from inside destructors or swap functions.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Why must destructors and move constructors be marked noexcept in C++?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Because throwing an exception during stack unwinding (when another exception is already active) triggers immediate std::terminate() and crashes the process. Move constructors must be noexcept so standard containers like std::vector can move elements safely during reallocation.

topics.title: std::optional & std::expected for Explicit Errors
topics.description: Modern error handling without exception overhead using std::optional (C++17) and std::expected (C++23).

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: std::optional<T> represents a value that may or may not exist (eliminating magic sentinel return values like -1 or null). std::expected<T, E> represents either a valid value T or an error E.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Exceptions should be reserved for exceptional failures (e.g. disk failure, out of memory). Expected domain failures (e.g. invalid user input, item not found) are better modeled explicitly in return types.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Return std::optional<User> for queries that can be empty. Return std::expected<Token, AuthError> for operations that can fail with specific error reasons.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Caller checks if (res.has_value()) or uses monadic operations (and_then, transform).

sections.title: 8. Real-world example

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use optional/expected for expected operational results (e.g. cache misses, validation failures).

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use optional for fatal system failures.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Expressive function signatures; zero runtime exception overhead.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Requires checking has_value() at call sites.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: std::optional (C++17), std::expected (C++23), Monadic operations.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Calling .value() on an empty optional without checking has_value() (throws std::bad_optional_access).

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the advantage of std::expected over returning error codes or throwing exceptions?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: std::expected forces callers to handle both the success value and error type at compile time with zero heap allocation or stack unwinding overhead.

topics.title: Exceptions vs Error Codes in Low-Level Design
topics.description: Architectural evaluation: Performance, stack unwinding latency, binary size, and domain error strategies.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: A structured evaluation of when to use C++ Exceptions vs Error Codes / Monadic Result types.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Low-latency systems (HFT, game engines) often disable C++ exceptions (-fno-exceptions) due to binary bloat and non-deterministic stack unwinding latency.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Use exceptions for rare, fatal system failures. Use error codes/expected for predictable domain logic branches.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Benchmark and align error handling with non-functional latency requirements.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Follow company/system coding standards (e.g. Google C++ Style Guide avoids exceptions).

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not mix unstructured error codes and exceptions randomly without architectural rules.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Clear error contracts and predictable runtime behavior.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Error codes can be ignored if not marked [[nodiscard]].

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Error Codes, [[nodiscard]], std::expected, C++ Exceptions.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Ignoring error code returns.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Why is the happy path faster with zero-cost exceptions, but the error path slower?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Zero-cost exceptions emit side tables (DWARF / SEH) that add zero instructions during normal execution. However, when an exception is thrown, the runtime must parse these tables and unwind the stack, which is orders of magnitude slower.
